newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peseta debt/interbank market closing report.
newsitem.headline: Peseta debt/interbank market closing report.

text.p: Spanish government bonds ended higher as they tracked foreign markets on Friday, although bonos lagged Italian Btps which were fuelled by the lira's likely re-entry to the ERM this weekend.
"We're following Btps, but we can't run so fast," a dealer in Madrid said.
At 1610 GMT while bono futures were up 16 basis points to 111.17, their Italian counterparts were up 65 bps to 127.92.
"Btps have more good news than us to factor in. November inflation, likely heavy reduction in rates and the lira's re-entry," said Henrik Lumholdt, economist with Bank of America.
"At the same time in Spain, we don't expect anything in particular, apart from November CPI (scheduled on December 13). So it's more likely BTPs will benefit the most," he added.
The 10-year spread over Bunds ended the day around 132 bps, not far off 131 bps, an all-time low set on Wednesday.
But the spread over Italy was trading at over 40 basis points, to where it had rebounded yesterday.
"Yesterday, bonos were the star," said Robert Huw, strategist at Natwest in London. "It might be the start of a new trend in which bonos outperform BTPs in the next two months."
Others dealers were not ruling out profit-taking in Btps.
"Both markets seem overbought and overpriced to me. But Spain is even more expensive," said Alessandro Ceccaroni, dealer at UBS in London.
"If anything I'd sell Spain," he added.
Growing expectations of the lira's re-entry to the ERM were fueled by a remark by Italy's Treasury Minister.

He said that the lira would re-join the monetary system before the end of November. Later a source said European Union monetary officials were preparing for a monetary committee meeting on Saturday to discuss the matter.
The peseta traded little changed at 84.14/4.16 versus the mark.
Earlier this morning the Bank of Spain was seen checking peseta rates versus the mark.
"I don't think the Bank of Spain really wants the peseta to strengthen any more than that," an analyst said.
